title: Phishing: Hacking the Human
objective: After this level you can explain why phishing works by rushing and tricking people rather than breaking code, and spot its signs.
summary: Phishing is social engineering: messages posing as someone you trust, pulling levers like urgency. Break the rush and verify another way; passkeys defeat even perfect fakes.

cards.headline: Why pick a lock when someone will hand you the key?
cards.body: Level 55's math is brutal to break. A person in a hurry is not. Phishing goes after the human, not the code.

cards.headline: Hacking the human
cards.body: Security people call it social engineering: tricking someone into revealing information, such as a password, that can be used to attack systems. Phishing is social engineering by message. An email, a text or a fake website poses as an organisation you trust, and fishes for your details.

cards.headline: Five levers
cards.body: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre lists the levers scammers pull: authority (a message that seems to come from your bank or the tax office), urgency (pay now or face a fine), emotion (fear or curiosity), scarcity (a deal about to vanish) and current events (whatever is in the news). Every lever does the same job: it pushes you to act before you think.

cards.headline: Slow down and go around
cards.body: So the defense is to break the rush. CISA's advice: if a request seems odd, contact the company directly, using contact details you already have, never the ones in the message. Technology helps too. Level 54's passkeys are bound to the real website, so even a flawless fake page gets nothing it can use.

cards.headline: Phish: spotted
learned: Social engineering tricks people into revealing information
Phishing poses as someone you trust to fish for details
Authority, urgency, emotion, scarcity and current events rush you
Verify through contact details you already have

questions.prompt: One of the five levers the UK's NCSC says scammers pull is _____.

options.label: encryption
options.rationale: Encryption protects data; it is not a scammer's lever.

options.label: compression
options.rationale: Compression shrinks files; it is not on the list.

questions.explanation: The NCSC's five: authority, urgency, emotion, scarcity and current events.

questions.prompt: Match each lever scammers pull with an example of it.

pairs.right: Seems to come from your bank

questions.explanation: Authority is a message that seems to come from your bank, emotion means fear or curiosity, scarcity is a deal about to vanish, and current events means whatever is in the news.

questions.prompt: Why can't even a flawless fake login page steal a Level 54 passkey?

options.label: Passkeys are too long to type into a fake page
options.rationale: You never type a passkey at all.

options.label: Fake pages cannot use HTTPS
options.rationale: Phishing sites can use HTTPS too.

options.label: The passkey is bound to the real website
Passkeys change every 30 seconds
options.rationale: That describes app codes, not passkeys.

questions.explanation: A passkey is cryptographically bound to the real site, so a look-alike page gets nothing it can use.
